newsitem.title: USA: ADM settlement seen as corporate governance gain.
newsitem.headline: ADM settlement seen as corporate governance gain.

text.p: A proposed settlement of shareholder lawsuits against directors of Archer Daniels Midland Co. marks a gain for advocates of corporate governance, legal experts and shareholders said.
"We tried to correct what we alleged were breaches of fiduciary duties," said Eugene Spector, an attorney whose firm represented ADM shareholders in the lawsuits.
U.S. District Judge Harold Baker on Friday gave preliminary approval to a settlement of shareholder suits against certain ADM directors.
The shareholders alleged ADM directors did not prevent the activities that led to the company's 1996 guilty plea to price-fixing charges.
"The real important relief is the corporate therapeutics that we've been able to negotitate as part of this settlement," Spector said in a telephone interview.

Terms of the proposed settlement approved in the Illinois court call for ADM directors to pay $8 million to the company to settle the claims. In addition, directors of ADM agreed to adopt several corporate governance measures.

Institutional shareholders had been pressing for corporate governance reform at ADM since a federal probe of alleged price fixing in the food and feed additives industry came to light about two years ago. As a result of that investigation, ADM pleaded guilty to two counts of price fixing and agreed to pay $100 million in fines.
"This settlement ... may close the books for the time being," said Edward Durkin, director of special programmes for the United Brotherhood of Carpenters, which holds about 770,000 ADM shares.
Demands made by institutional shareholders in the past include the appointment of directors with no personal or business ties to ADM and greater accountability for the board.
Durkin said the settlement coupled with the naming of a new chief executive officer last month at ADM signals a culture change at the agribusiness giant.
"We have real solid governance reform," Durkin said. "It's time for shareholders to step back on the aggressive advocacy and let this company meet the challenge."

Analysts said the court ruling removes a potential distraction for management. "The company is moving all these sorts of issues behind to get back to business," said David Nelson, an analyst at NatWest Securities.

The corporate governance measures include a new definition of an outside director which precludes an employee or family member from taking the position. ADM directors also agreed that its audit committee would oversee, among other things, compliance with federal securities laws and determine whether the company is engaged in anticompetitive activities.
"ADM was behind the curve on these issues and this will bring them closer to what other companies are doing," said Robert Thompson, professor of law at Washington University in St. Louis.

Company officials were not immediately available to provide information about whether ADM's directors are insured for the costs of the settlement. According to the settlement, ADM will pay legal fees incurred by shareholders out of the $8 million.
